opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a real gap between what people imagine and what's actually happening in operating rooms. Most people hear "robot surgery" and picture a machine making decisions on its own, but systems like the da Vinci are really teleoperated. They're extraordinarily sophisticated puppets. The surgeon is in full control every second, and the robot just scales and filters their hand motions.

Going from that to full autonomy is hard for a few reasons. The first is perception. The human body is soft, wet, and deformable. Tissue moves when you touch it, it bleeds, it gets obscured by fluids and smoke, and no two patients are the same. Robots are actually quite good in structured environments like a factory, where the parts are rigid and you know exactly where everything is. Surgery is the opposite of that. You're dealing with enormous uncertainty in exactly where things are and how they'll respond when you push on them.

The second issue is what I'd call the long tail of rare events. A surgeon might do a procedure a thousand times, and then on the thousand-and-first, something unexpected happens: an anatomical variation, an unexpected bleed. Humans are remarkably good at improvising in those moments, drawing on intuition and common sense built over a lifetime. Current AI systems are quite brittle when they encounter situations outside their training distribution, and in surgery, those are precisely the moments where the stakes are highest.

The third is data. People point to the enormous progress in language models, which were trained on essentially the whole internet. But we don't have anything like that for physical manipulation, and especially not for surgery. Surgical video exists, but it doesn't capture forces, tactile feedback, or the surgeon's reasoning. That data gap is very significant, and it's one reason I've been somewhat skeptical of claims that robotics is about to have its "ChatGPT moment."

Then there are the regulatory and liability questions. If an autonomous system makes an error, who's responsible? Hospitals and regulators are, rightly, very conservative.

So where I think we'll see progress is in what I'd call augmented dexterity rather than full autonomy: robots taking over specific, well-defined subtasks like suturing, or suctioning, or retracting tissue, under the supervision of a surgeon who can step in at any moment. It's a bit like how cars have gradually gotten lane-keeping and adaptive cruise control. The human stays in the loop, and the robot handles the tedious, repetitive parts. I think that's both more realistic and, frankly, a better model for how humans and robots should work together.

r001.rationale: The response says errors have high stakes and that hospitals and regulators are conservative, but it does not identify low tolerance for small errors as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says tissue can bleed and become obscured by fluids and smoke, directly explaining the perception difficulty.

r003.rationale: It mentions surgeons’ intuition and common sense, but does not explain how they use prior anatomical knowledge to interpret what they encounter.

r004.rationale: It describes the body as soft and deformable and explains that tissue moves when touched, making its location and response uncertain to robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's funny, because people have been predicting it for a long time. I remember when the da Vinci system came out around 2000, and people said, "Oh, within ten years surgeons will be obsolete, the robot will just do it." And here we are, decades later, and there are thousands of these robots in hospitals, but every single one of them is still teleoperated. There's a human surgeon sitting at a console controlling every motion. The robot never does anything on its own.

And I think the reason is that surgery is just an extraordinarily hard physical problem. When you look inside the body, it's not like a factory floor where everything's rigid and in a known position. Everything is deformable. Tissue stretches, it slides, it bleeds, it's covered in fluid, it's specular so it reflects light in weird ways. Organs move when the patient breathes. So perception is incredibly hard. The robot has to figure out where things are, and that's much harder than it sounds when nothing holds still and everything looks slightly different from one patient to the next.

Then there's the manipulation side. Even something that seems trivial, like tying a suture, involves a thread that's a thin, flexible object, and modelling the dynamics of that is really difficult. In our lab we've spent years on suturing, just the needle-passing and knot-tying part, and we've gotten to the point where we can do it in a lab setting on a phantom, but it's still not as reliable as a good surgeon. And "pretty reliable" isn't good enough when the consequences of a mistake are catastrophic. If a warehouse robot drops a box, you pick it up. If a surgical robot nicks an artery, somebody could die.

And that points to the deeper issue, which is that the variability is in the tails. Every patient's anatomy is a little different. There are adhesions from previous surgeries, there's unexpected bleeding, there are anomalies you only see once in a thousand cases. Surgeons are trained to recognise those and adapt. Robots are very good at the central, repeatable cases, but they're very bad at the rare ones, and in surgery it's the rare ones that matter.

So I've become sort of a skeptic about full autonomy in surgery, at least in the near term. What I think is much more realistic is what I'd call augmented dexterity. The surgeon stays in charge, but the robot takes over certain subtasks, like suturing or holding retraction or doing a very steady, repetitive motion, while the surgeon supervises and steps in when something unexpected happens. That's a bit like the trajectory we've seen with aircraft, where autopilot handles the routine parts but the pilot is still there. I think that's where the real near-term gains are, and frankly I think it's the safer path too.

r001.rationale: It says “pretty reliable” is not good enough because a surgical mistake such as nicking an artery could kill someone.

r002.rationale: It mentions bleeding and says perception is difficult, but does not explain that blood obscures the surgical field.

r003.rationale: It says surgeons recognize rare anomalies and adapt, but does not explain that they use prior anatomical knowledge to interpret what they encounter.

r004.rationale: It describes tissue as deformable, stretching and sliding, and connects that variability to the difficulty of perception.

astra-6.text:
Well, one of the fundamental difficulties is that the body isn’t a predictable environment. If you’re assembling a car, you can arrange for the parts to be in very precise locations. In surgery, every patient is different, and the tissue moves and deforms as you interact with it. When you pull on one part, other parts move, and often you can’t see exactly what’s happening underneath.

So it’s not just a question of getting the robot’s motions accurate enough. It has to interpret what it’s seeing, reason about uncertainty, and respond when something unexpected happens. A surgeon brings an enormous amount of experience to that. They know when to proceed, when to change their approach, and when to stop.

I think we can make progress by automating particular subtasks, with a surgeon supervising and able to take over. But going from that to a system that can handle an entire operation, including the unusual situations where a mistake could be catastrophic—that’s a much bigger challenge.

r001.rationale: It says mistakes in unusual situations could be catastrophic, but does not identify surgery’s low tolerance for small errors as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention blood obscuring the surgical field.

r003.rationale: It describes surgeons’ experience and judgment, but does not say they use prior anatomical knowledge to interpret what they encounter.

r004.rationale: It explains that tissue moves and deforms during interaction, moving other parts and making it hard to see what is happening—an obstacle for robotic perception.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, surgery is a very challenging environment for a robot because the world you’re working in is deformable. If you’re assembling a car, you can usually assume that a part has a particular shape and is in a fairly predictable location. In surgery, when you pull on a piece of tissue, everything around it moves. And every patient is different.

There’s also a tremendous amount of uncertainty. You can’t necessarily see what’s behind a surface, and blood can obscure your view. A surgeon is constantly interpreting what’s happening and adjusting, drawing on experience that can be very difficult to articulate as a set of rules.

We’ve made progress on automating individual tasks, like moving a needle through tissue. But doing a task under controlled conditions is very different from handling an entire operation, including the unexpected things that might happen. If something starts bleeding, you need to recognise that, understand what caused it, and decide how to respond safely.

So I think the useful direction is to work with surgeons: give them tools that can take over particular subtasks while they maintain oversight. That can be valuable well before we have a robot that could perform a whole operation on its own.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and responding safely to complications, but does not identify low tolerance for small errors as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says blood can obscure the surgeon’s view, making it harder to interpret what is happening.

r003.rationale: It mentions surgeons drawing on experience, but does not explain that they use prior knowledge of anatomy to interpret what they encounter.

r004.rationale: It says tissue is deformable and movement in surrounding tissue makes surgery challenging, but does not clearly state that this makes tissue difficult for robots to perceive.
